# A Tour of Agents

> Interactive browser-based course teaching how AI agent systems work. 9 lessons, 60 lines of Python, no framework required.

## What This Site Is

An educational course that progressively builds a complete AI agent from scratch in plain Python. Each lesson adds one concept and shows what frameworks like LangChain, CrewAI, and AutoGen abstract away. Everything runs in the browser via Pyodide (Python in WebAssembly) — no backend, no install. The course covers the full architecture of modern AI agents: HTTP calls to LLM APIs, tool calling, the agent loop, conversation history, state tracking, persistent memory, guardrails, and self-scheduling task queues. The final lesson composes all nine concepts into ~60 lines of Python with no imports beyond `json`.

## Lessons

1. Agent = Function (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/agent-function)
   An agent is a function that sends an HTTP POST to an LLM API's /chat/completions endpoint and returns the response. The lesson builds `ask_llm()` from scratch, showing that the system prompt controls behavior and the messages array is the conversation. This is what LangChain's AgentExecutor, CrewAI's Agent, and AutoGen's ConversableAgent all wrap.

2. Tools = Dict (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/tools)
   Tool calling means the LLM returns a structured JSON request naming a function and its arguments, and your code dispatches it via `tools[name](**args)`. The lesson builds a tools dictionary with `add` and `upper` functions, writes JSON Schema descriptions for the LLM, and shows the dispatch pattern. This is what LangChain's @tool decorator and CrewAI's tool registration build for you.

3. The Agent Loop (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/agent-loop)
   The agent loop is a while loop that calls the LLM, checks for tool_calls in the response, executes matching tools, appends results (with tool_call_id) to the messages array, and repeats until the LLM stops requesting tools. This is the core runtime of LangChain's AgentExecutor and the most important lesson in the course. It enables multi-step behavior like Claude searching files, reading them, then searching again.

4. Conversation (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/conversation)
   Conversation history is the messages array moved outside the agent function so it persists across calls. Each user message is appended before the loop, each assistant response after. This is why ChatGPT remembers your last message and why "New Chat" forgets — new chat creates a new empty list. LangChain calls this ConversationBufferMemory.

5. State = Dict (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/state)
   State is a dictionary updated inside the agent loop that tracks structured metadata alongside the conversation — which tools ran, how many turns elapsed, what results were produced. This is how Claude shows "Searched 5 files" or ChatGPT shows "Analyzed data." LangGraph calls these "state channels" with typed reducers; here it is a plain dict.

6. Memory (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/memory)
   Memory persists information across separate agent runs by maintaining a dict outside the conversation, injected into the system prompt at the start of each call. The LLM saves to it via a `remember()` tool — just another entry in the tools dict. This is how ChatGPT Memory knows your name across sessions. Mem0, Zep, and LangChain's ConversationSummaryMemory are variations on this pattern.

7. Policy (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/policy)
   Policy adds two gates around the agent loop: an input gate that blocks dangerous requests before they reach the LLM (saving tokens and preventing harm), and an output gate that redacts the LLM's response before the user sees it. Each gate is a list of rule functions that return True to pass or a string explanation to block. This is the architecture behind Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails, and ChatGPT's content refusal system.

8. Self-Scheduling (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/self-scheduling)
   Self-scheduling gives the agent a `schedule_followup` tool that appends new tasks to a queue. An outer scheduler loop pops tasks and runs the agent on each one until the queue drains or a budget cap (max_tasks) is hit. This creates two levels of iteration: the scheduler picks what to work on, the inner agent loop decides how. CrewAI calls this delegation, AutoGen calls it nested chats, and ChatGPT deep research uses this pattern to spawn sub-tasks.

9. The Whole Thing (https://tinyagents.dev/lessons/the-whole-thing)
   The final lesson composes all eight previous concepts into a single ~60-line Python agent: HTTP POST to LLM (L1), tool dispatch via dict (L2), while-loop agent loop (L3), conversation history (L4), state tracking dict (L5), memory injection in system prompt (L6), input/output policy gates (L7), and self-scheduling task queue (L8). No imports beyond json and pyfetch. This is the same architecture as LangChain + LangGraph + Guardrails AI combined.

## Framework Comparisons

- LangChain vs Plain Python (https://tinyagents.dev/compare/langchain)
  Side-by-side comparison of LangChain's AgentExecutor, @tool decorator, ConversationBufferMemory, LangGraph state channels, and output parsers against their plain Python equivalents. LangChain's 200+ classes across chains, agents, memory, and output parsers each map to a few lines of Python. The comparison covers when LangChain adds value (multiple provider integrations, vector store RAG pipelines, LangSmith observability) and when plain Python is simpler.

- CrewAI vs Plain Python (https://tinyagents.dev/compare/crewai)
  Compares CrewAI's Agent/Task/Crew model to plain Python functions. CrewAI organizes work into Agents with roles, goals, and backstories, Tasks that define work items, and Crews that orchestrate execution (sequential or hierarchical). In plain Python, an Agent is a function with a system prompt, task delegation is a list processed in a for-loop, and hierarchical execution is a manager agent that decides which sub-agent to call. CrewAI helps when role separation genuinely improves prompt quality.

- AutoGen vs Plain Python (https://tinyagents.dev/compare/autogen)
  Compares Microsoft AutoGen's ConversableAgent, GroupChat, and nested chats to plain Python. AutoGen models agents as conversational participants that alternate turns on a shared message history. In plain Python, two-agent chat is a while loop alternating between agent functions, GroupChat adds a speaker selection step, and nested chats are a function call that pauses the main conversation to run a sub-loop. AutoGen excels at dynamic multi-agent debates; for single-agent tool-calling, plain Python is significantly simpler.

- OpenAI Agents SDK vs Plain Python (https://tinyagents.dev/compare/openai-agents-sdk)
  Compares OpenAI's Agents SDK (formerly Swarm) to plain Python. The SDK provides Agent, Runner, handoffs, and guardrails with auto-schema generation from Python type hints. It is the thinnest framework compared here — Runner.run() is a while loop, handoffs are an if-statement routing to different agent functions, and guardrails are validation function lists. The main unique feature is auto-schema generation; the plain Python version is barely longer for single-agent setups.

## Blog

- How AI Agents Actually Work (https://tinyagents.dev/blog/how-ai-agents-work)
  Explains the full AI agent architecture in plain language: an agent is a function that POSTs to an LLM API, tools are a dictionary of callables dispatched by name, the agent loop is a while loop that exits when the LLM stops requesting tools, conversation is a list that grows, and memory is a dict injected into the system prompt. Covers every major concept from LangChain, CrewAI, and AutoGen and shows the ~60-line plain Python equivalent.

- You Don't Need LangChain (https://tinyagents.dev/blog/langchain-vs-plain-python)
  A side-by-side breakdown of LangChain's AgentExecutor (a while loop), @tool decorator (a dict entry), and ConversationBufferMemory (a list) against their plain Python equivalents. Argues that LangChain's 200+ classes add value for production integrations (multi-provider support, vector store retrieval, LangSmith) but that for learning, prototyping, or straightforward agents, plain Python is clearer and more debuggable.

- LLM Tool Calling Explained (https://tinyagents.dev/blog/what-is-tool-calling)
  Technical explanation of how LLM tool calling (also called function calling) works at the API level. You send a tools array with JSON Schema descriptions, the LLM responds with tool_calls instead of text content, you execute the function and send back a message with role "tool" and the tool_call_id. The dispatch pattern is `tools[name](**args)` — the same pattern as an Express router or Redux reducer. Multi-step tool use is a while loop over this protocol.

- Build vs Buy AI Agent Framework (https://tinyagents.dev/blog/build-vs-buy-ai-agent-framework)
  A decision framework for choosing between LangChain/CrewAI/AutoGen and building from scratch. Breaks framework value into three categories: wiring (connecting to providers and stores), patterns (pre-built agent loop, memory, guardrails), and ecosystem (LangSmith, deployment, community). Category 2 is where most teams get burned — the patterns are simple enough that the abstraction costs more than it saves. Recommends understanding the fundamentals first, then deciding whether the framework's integration surface area justifies the dependency.

## Key Technical Details

- Python runs client-side via Pyodide (WebAssembly)
- LLM calls use the OpenAI-compatible chat completions API format
- Trace events emitted via print("__TRACE__:...") from Python, parsed in TypeScript
- Interactive debugger with play/pause/step controls and turn-aware replay
- Works with mock LLM responses (no API key) or real providers (Groq, OpenAI, Anthropic via OpenRouter)
- API keys stored in browser localStorage only, never sent to any server
- The complete agent (lesson 9) uses only json and pyfetch — no external Python dependencies
